newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban battle allies and foes in northern city.
newsitem.headline: Taleban battle allies and foes in northern city.

text.p: The Taleban Islamic militia fought street battles with its supposed allies as well as with Shi'ite Moslem foes in the newly-conquered northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday.

Bursts of machinegun fire ripped through the streets and explosions from heavier weapons rocked the city through the night and into Wednesday morning. Black smoke from a burning building rose from the centre.
U.N. officials were discussing plans to evacuate international staff, but it was not immediately known if they would be able to drive to the border with Uzbekistan or fly to Pakistan.

Fighting erupted on Tuesday afternoon, just after a meeting between Taleban leaders and an ethnic Uzbek general, Abdul Malik, whose troops were supposed to be operating jointly with the Islamic militia.

Witnesses said the clashes broke out when a Taleban column of tanks and armoured personnel carriers moved into the Shi'ite northern district of Saidabad to collect weapons from suspected members of the opposition Hezb-i-Wahdat militia.
They said the column came under fire from Uzbek troops angered by the presence of the Taleban's mainly ethnic Pashtun zealots in the Uzbek-dominated northern capital.
Earlier on Tuesday, at least three Taleban fighters were killed by residents in Saidabad who said they were caught looting.
The Taleban arrived on Sunday, a day after General Malik's Uzbek soldiers captured the city and forced opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum to flee the country.
The Islamic militia, which has not experienced street fighting in its rapid advance across Afghanistan, is now locked in combat, with its supply lines looking precarious.
Most of the Taleban's black-turbanned warriors swept in from the northwestern province of Badghis across Dostum's former territory, which may now have turned hostile.
About 200 Taleban flew in on Tuesday from the southern city of Kandahar, headquarters of Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar.
Malik said his revolt against Dostum was in favour of the Taleban, and his troops first rode into Mazar-i-Sharif flying white Taleban flags from their vehicles.
The tension has remained high since the arrival of the Taleban, reflecting the bad blood between them and the Uzbeks, many of whom fought for the communist government that collapsed in April 1992.

The United Arab Emirates on Tuesday became the third nation to accord formal diplomatic recognition to the Taleban government, which was was set up after the militia, led by Islamic theology students, captured Kabul last September and which controls nearly 90 percent of the war-shattered country.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have already recognised the Taleban government.
The United States called on Tuesday for an end to fighting in Afghanistan but left unclear whether it would accord diplomatic recognition.
